    Key Points

    Week 1: Text and encoding

    • Each week has four blocks: Watch, Read & practise, Concepts Bridge and Build.
    • A string is a sequence of characters, counted from 0.
    • A slice [start:stop:step] makes a new string and stops before stop.
    • Strings cannot be changed; every method gives you a new string.
    • Tidy text first (lower, strip) before you count or compare it.
    • split makes a list of pieces; join puts them back together.
    • f-string format specs such as :>8 and :.2f line up columns.
    • Every character has a number; ASCII covers 128 of them.
    • UTF-8 stores each character in 1 to 4 bytes.
    • Always say which encoding a file uses; the wrong one gives garbled text.
    • Everything in a computer is stored as numbers.
    • A byte is a number from 0 to 255; hexadecimal is a short way to write it.
    • Small, pure functions that take text and return values are easy to test.

    Week 2: Files and structured data

    • Each week has four blocks: Watch, Read & practise, Concepts Bridge and Build.
    • with closes the file for you, even if something goes wrong.
    • The mode “r” reads, “w” replaces and “a” adds to the end.
    • Use strip() to remove the newline from each line.
    • Use the csv module, not split(“,”), because values can contain commas.
    • Open CSV files with newline=“” .
    • Everything you read from a CSV file is a string; convert it yourself.
    • JSON looks like Python dictionaries and lists.
    • json.dump and json.load work with files; dumps and loads work with strings.
    • JSON cannot hold your own objects until you turn them into dictionaries.
    • A log line holds an address, a time, a request, a status code and a size.
    • A 401 means a login failed; a 404 means the page was not found.
    • Check that a line has enough parts before you use it.
    • Data from outside may be wrong, damaged or hostile.
    • JSON and CSV hold data only. pickle and eval() can run code.
    • Check what you load before you trust it.
    • Read, check and convert data in small functions; keep file handling in main().

    Week 3: Validation, integrity and a simple cipher

    • Each week has four blocks: Watch, Read & practise, Concepts Bridge and Build.
    • Validation means checking data before you use it.
    • An allow-list (what is allowed) is safer than a block-list (what is banned).
    • Report every problem at once so the user can fix them together.
    • A hash is a fixed-length fingerprint of data.
    • The same input always gives the same hash; a tiny change gives a very different one.
    • You cannot work back from a hash to the data.
    • The Caesar cipher shifts every letter by a fixed number.
    • It is a teaching cipher. It is not secure and must never protect real data.
    • Encoding represents data. It is not security.
    • Encryption hides data and can be reversed with the key.
    • Hashing gives a fingerprint and cannot be reversed.
    • Never type or save a real password in a practice program.

    Week 4: Libraries and NumPy

    • Each week has four blocks: Watch, Read & practise, Concepts Bridge and Build.
    • A virtual environment is a private set of packages for one project.
    • Install with python -m pip install, inside the project.
    • Install only well-known packages and check the spelling of the name.
    • An array holds numbers of one type in one block.
    • Arithmetic on an array works on every item at once (vectorised).
    • A boolean mask such as a[a > 5] picks the items that pass a test.
    • The standard deviation measures how spread out values are.
    • axis=0 works down each column; axis=1 works along each row.
    • A z-score above 3 is unusual. That is a reason to look closer, not proof of a problem.
    • An array holds one type of number in one block, so the loop runs in fast compiled code.
    • For small data, mixed types or a short script, a list and a loop can be clearer.
    • An unusual value is a reason to look closer, not proof of an attack.

    Week 5: Pandas

    • Each week has four blocks: Watch, Read & practise, Concepts Bridge and Build.
    • A DataFrame is a table with named columns; a Series is one column.
    • head, info and describe show you the data before you work on it.
    • df[df[“status”] == 404] keeps the rows that pass the test.
    • Put each condition in brackets when you combine them.
    • value_counts() counts how often each value appears.
    • groupby splits the rows into groups, applies a calculation and combines the results.
    • size() counts rows; count() counts values that are not missing.
    • A missing value shows as NaN.
    • Totals and means skip missing values unless you fill them.
    • Write down every cleaning step you take.
    • Record every cleaning step you take.
    • Collect only what you need, use it for its purpose, keep it secure and remove it when it is no longer needed.
    • This course uses synthetic data only.
    • A pattern in a log is a reason to look closer, not proof.

    Week 6: Charts and capstone

    • Each week has four blocks: Watch, Read & practise, Concepts Bridge and Build.
    • Every chart needs a title and labelled axes with units.
    • savefig saves the chart; show opens a window.
    • Use a line chart for change over time, a bar chart to compare groups and a histogram for the spread of one measure.
    • Bars should start at zero.
    • Start from the question, not from the chart.
    • Finish with one sentence that says what the chart shows.
    • The person who makes a chart is responsible for the impression it gives.
    • Start bars at zero, label axes with units and compare rates when totals would mislead.
    • Choose the chart that suits the question, and make it honest.
